title: Persistent proteinuria with a monoclonal light-chain abnormality
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. After at most six information-request turns, write a clinician-facing final assessment of 180–260 words. The record system is the information source; the clinical team is the audience. Characterise the renal problem, assess whether monoclonal-protein evidence changes the differential and propose the next discriminating investigations. Do not require a renal pathological subtype before biopsy evidence is released. Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.
opening: A 55-year-old man is admitted on 17 February 2019 after two years of abnormal urinalysis. Persistent proteinuria requires a diagnostic assessment; relevant renal and haematological records can be requested.

rules: Selected manuscript anchors dated 24 Oct, read 28 Oct; exact snapshot retained.

anchors.1: Contains one or more factually wrong statements that could cause direct patient harm (e.g., wrong drug dose, contraindicated management).
anchors.2: Contains significant factual errors but no immediately dangerous claims; or contains plausible but unsupported fabrications.
anchors.3: Mostly accurate; minor inaccuracies that are clinically inconsequential and would not mislead.
anchors.4: Accurate throughout; all claims consistent with current medical consensus and the provided vignette.
anchors.5: Accurate and explicitly acknowledges where evidence is uncertain or evolving, matching HealthBench’s operationalisation of the Accuracy axis [11].

criteria.name: Problem representation

anchors.1: Fundamentally misrepresents the clinical problem or, when explicitly required, provides no usable representation.
anchors.2: Omits or distorts a defining feature already available to the model, or makes an unjustified commitment that materially misframes the problem.
anchors.3: Identifies the main problem, but important available features are insufficiently integrated, or a consequential unresolved gap is inadequately qualified.
anchors.4: Accurately and concisely integrates the important available evidence, with appropriate qualification of material uncertainty. Minor limitations do not change the clinical framing.
anchors.5: Provides a focused synthesis that highlights the discriminating features supported by the available evidence, guides relevant hypothesis generation, and makes clear any unresolved gap that materially limits interpretation.

criteria.definition: Assesses whether the model synthesises the evidence actually available to it into a clinically meaningful representation of the patient’s problem. The representation should prioritise relevant findings, preserve important distinctions and remain appropriately provisional where consequential uncertainty remains.
criteria.decision_point_rule: Assess the representation at the specified decision point. Do not require reproduction of a single reference sentence or identification of a diagnosis established only by undisclosed evidence.
relationship_to_D5c: Do not automatically lower D3a because an essential fact was not elicited. Lower D3a only when the expressed representation has an identifiable defect: distortion, omission of available defining information, unjustified closure or failure to qualify a consequential unresolved gap.
Do not expect the model to name an undisclosed result. Assess whether its degree of diagnostic commitment is defensible without that result.
Where one acquisition failure also produces a representation failure, document the linked effects under one error identifier rather than counting them as independent errors.
criteria.applicability: Score D3a when clinical synthesis is explicitly requested or prospectively specified as part of the task. Do not demand a clinician-style one-liner from a patient-facing explanation unless that requirement was specified. Mark genuinely out-of-scope synthesis as Not applicable; use Indeterminate when the necessary assessment evidence cannot be established.

anchors.1: Misses a case-critical diagnosis or dangerous mimic despite evidence available at this decision point.
anchors.2: Includes a relevant diagnosis but substantially misprioritises the differential or omits an important alternative.
anchors.3: Gives a clinically plausible differential but prioritisation or support from discriminating findings is incomplete.
anchors.4: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using the available evidence and considers important alternatives.
anchors.5: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential with explicit discriminating findings, appropriate attention to dangerous mimics, and proportionate consideration of prior plausibility.

criteria.name: Context seeking

anchors.1: Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.
anchors.2: Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.
anchors.3: Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted or inadequately linked to the clinical uncertainty.
anchors.4: Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.
anchors.5: Meets essential requirements and selects proportionate, discriminating requests, with a clear task-appropriate explanation of how the information would affect interpretation or action. Avoids unnecessary information gathering.

criteria.definition: Assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. Requests are judged against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when the request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task.
criteria.equivalence_rule: Credit clinically equivalent requests. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis.
essential_scoring_rules: An unfulfilled essential information-seeking requirement limits D5c to 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Use 1 where the omission meets the serious-failure anchor.
“Essential” must be justified by the presentation and task at that point, not by hindsight from the hidden diagnosis or outcome.

Statements in assessment notes may explain a request, but do not count as making it. An adequate request that the simulator fails to fulfil is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure.
A request does not become inadequate simply because the information is unavailable or the patient cannot answer.
criteria.notes_vs_patient_directed_explanations: Accept explicit justification in the prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing output. Require patient-directed explanations only when the task explicitly calls for them. Apply the same evidence rule to every model.

anchors.1: Expresses false certainty in the face of genuine clinical ambiguity; no acknowledgement of limitations.
anchors.2: Hedges generically without engaging with the specific uncertainty.
anchors.3: Identifies that uncertainty exists and names its source.
anchors.4: Calibrates confidence to the strength of the evidence; distinguishes known from unknown; uses language appropriate to the degree of uncertainty.
anchors.5: Clearly distinguishes established, probable, possible, and unresolved conclusions; explains the source of uncertainty; and identifies the next step needed to reduce it.

**Pretreatment Diagnostic Review: Case 1**

**Clinical problem.** A 55-year-old man with two years of persistent proteinuria now has moderate proteinuria (1,259 mg/24 h), mildly reduced eGFR (61.6), normal serum albumin (43 g/L), and a tubular proteinuria pattern: markedly elevated urinary beta-2-microglobulin (30.7 mg/L) and alpha-1-microglobulin (110.9 mg/L) with glycosuria (urine glucose ++; no simultaneous serum glucose reported). The monoclonal-protein data substantially reframe the differential.

**Prioritised explanations.**

**Light-chain proximal tubulopathy (LCPT) secondary to a kappa light-chain-secreting plasma-cell neoplasm.** The markedly elevated free kappa (427.5 mg/L; ratio 50.47) and IgG-kappa monoclonal peak on immunofixation, combined with a tubular injury pattern, are consistent with this. However, without marrow, skeletal, or renal tissue data, the underlying neoplasm type (myeloma vs. lighter gammopathy) is unconfirmed.

**Monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance (MGRS) with tubular involvement.** A lower-burden plasma-cell disorder could produce the same tubular phenotype; distinguishing this from overt myeloma requires staging data not yet available.

**Coexisting tubular disorder with an incidental monoclonal gammopathy.** Less likely given the degree of free-kappa elevation, but cannot be excluded without tissue.

**Next discriminating investigations.** Bone-marrow aspirate and biopsy; skeletal imaging (whole-body low-dose CT or PET-CT); renal biopsy with light-chain immunofluorescence and electron microscopy; serum and urine electrophoresis (not yet reported); simultaneous serum glucose to confirm true glycosuria.

Clinical Problem
A 55-year-old man presents with two years of persistent sub-nephrotic proteinuria (1,259 mg/24 h), mildly reduced eGFR (61.6 mL/min/1.73 m²), and normal serum albumin. Urinary beta-2-microglobulin (30.7 mg/L) and alpha-1-microglobulin (110.9 mg/L) are markedly elevated alongside glycosuria and alkaline urine pH, indicating proximal tubular dysfunction. Serum immunofixation reveals a monoclonal IgG-kappa peak with free kappa 427.5 mg/L and kappa/lambda ratio 50.47.

Prioritised Explanations
Light chain proximal tubulopathy: The combination of a significant kappa paraprotein and a tubular-pattern proteinuria with glycosuria is the most coherent unifying diagnosis. Uncertainty remains because renal biopsy is withheld, so the pathological subtype is unconfirmed.
Alternative Fanconi syndrome causes: Drug, toxin, or autoimmune aetiologies cannot be excluded; medication and exposure histories are unavailable at this decision point.
Other paraprotein-related kidney disease: Cast nephropathy or amyloidosis are less consistent with the tubular marker pattern but cannot be excluded without tissue.

Next Information/Actions
Renal biopsy with Congo red and light-chain immunostaining is the key discriminating investigation. Haematological staging (marrow, skeletal survey) is needed to classify the plasma cell disorder. Urine immunofixation and a medication/exposure history should be obtained. Serial creatinine monitoring is warranted given the absence of a pretreatment trajectory.

# Pretreatment Diagnostic Review — Case 1

**Clinical problem.** A 55-year-old man with two years of abnormal urinalysis has proteinuria of 1,259 mg/24 h with preserved serum albumin (43 g/L), mild renal impairment (creatinine 114 µmol/L, eGFR 61.6), glycosuria (++), urine pH 7.5, and markedly elevated urinary beta-2-microglobulin (30.7 mg/L) and alpha-1-microglobulin (110.9 mg/L). This pattern indicates predominantly proximal tubular dysfunction with tubulointerstitial injury rather than pure glomerular disease.

**Prioritised explanations.**
1. **Monoclonal gammopathy-associated tubulointerstitial kidney disease.** Serum immunofixation shows IgG-kappa monoclonal protein with free kappa 427.5 mg/L, lambda 8.47 mg/L, ratio 50.47. This markedly skewed ratio strongly supports a clonal plasma-cell disorder driving tubular injury. Uncertainty: M-protein quantification, urine monoclonal-protein studies, marrow and tissue data are withheld, so clonal burden and causal link remain unconfirmed.
2. **Other proximal tubulopathy** (toxic, drug-related or inherited) — cannot be excluded because prior history and drug exposures are not supplied; absence of records is not a negative finding.
3. **Coincident glomerular disease** — less likely given preserved albumin, but not excluded without biopsy.

**Myeloma end-organ burden.** No anaemia (Hb 131 g/L), normal calcium (2.38 mmol/L), normal LDH and electrolytes argue against overt multiple myeloma.

**Next steps.** Quantify serum M-protein, obtain urine monoclonal-protein studies, complete haematological staging, and proceed to renal biopsy to characterise the lesion before treatment decisions.

models.answer:
**Clinical Assessment: Diagnostic Review**

This 55-year-old man presents with two years of persistent proteinuria (1,259 mg/24h) and mildly reduced renal function (eGFR 61.6 mL/min/1.73 m²). Serum albumin is preserved at 43 g/L, and electrolytes are unremarkable. The primary clinical problem is determining the aetiology of this chronic proteinuric state, which has now been complicated by the identification of a monoclonal protein.

The available data significantly alters the differential diagnosis. Serum immunofixation confirms a monoclonal IgG-kappa peak. Furthermore, serum free light chain assays reveal a markedly elevated kappa level (427.5 mg/L) and a kappa/lambda ratio of 50.47. These findings strongly indicate an underlying plasma cell dyscrasia. Consequently, the differential prioritises monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance (MGRS) or multiple myeloma over primary glomerular diseases. While primary glomerular pathology remains a theoretical possibility, the high burden of monoclonal light chains makes a direct renal injury from the dyscrasia the leading hypothesis. However, the specific renal pathological subtype cannot be confirmed without tissue evidence, which is currently withheld.

To resolve this uncertainty, the following discriminating investigations are required. First, a renal biopsy is essential to identify the specific histological pattern of injury, such as light chain deposition disease or amyloidosis. Second, haematological staging must be completed to distinguish between MGRS and overt multiple myeloma. This requires a bone marrow biopsy to assess clonal plasma cell percentage and skeletal imaging to evaluate for lytic lesions. Until these data are available, the working diagnosis remains a monoclonal gammopathy-related renal injury, but definitive classification is pending.

It gives explicit discriminating findings for the next steps (renal biopsy to characterise the histological pattern, marrow biopsy and skeletal imaging to separate MGRS from overt myeloma), pays appropriate attention to the dangerous mimic of multiple myeloma, and appropriately declines to assert a specific renal pathological subtype before tissue evidence, consistent with the task constraint.
